The Story of Jinendrabhakt

I pay homage to the Jina who bestows heaven and liberation, and write here the story of Jinendrabhakt, who practiced upaguhana — the limb of right faith that conceals the faults of fellow believers to protect the honour of the dharma.

In the city of Tamlipta, in the land of Gaud, there lived a wealthy merchant named Jinendrabhakt. True to his name — "Devotee of the Jina" — he was a man of genuine right faith who faithfully observed every duty of a householder. He built grand Jina temples, restored ancient ones, commissioned sacred images, and gave generously to the fourfold community.

His palace rose seven storeys high. On its topmost floor stood an exquisite Jina chapel housing a magnificent image of Lord Parshvanath, adorned with jewels. Three jewelled parasols crowned the image, and upon them glittered a priceless gem called Vaiduryamani, radiant beyond compare.

The Thief's Plan

In the city of Pataliputra, far to the north, lived a prince named Suvir — the son of Queen Susima of the same city. Though born to royalty, Suvir had fallen into a life of crime. When he heard of the wondrous gem in Jinendrabhakt's chapel, he summoned his companions and asked if anyone could bring it to him.

A thief named Suryak spoke up: "This is the simplest of tasks. Even if that gem sat on Indra's own head, I would have it in a moment." Such is the boastfulness of the wicked — the more depraved a person, the bolder their sins.

Suryak disguised himself as a Jain ascetic. He took up fasting and austerities until his body grew gaunt and thin. Travelling from town to town, deceiving people with his pious appearance, he eventually arrived in Tamlipta.

The Deception

Jinendrabhakt, being a truly devout man, felt great joy at the arrival of a holy figure. He rushed to pay his respects, and seeing the ascetic's emaciated body — the result of false austerities — his reverence only deepened. He brought the disguised thief to his own palace and installed him in the chapel as its guardian.

Even wise men can be deceived by cunning. When the fake ascetic laid eyes on the gem, his heart leapt with greed — just as a goldsmith's eyes light up at the sight of gold in a customer's hands.

Jinendrabhakt, suspecting nothing, departed on a sea voyage, leaving the chapel in the ascetic's care.

The Theft and the Pursuit

The moment Jinendrabhakt left, the thief struck. At midnight he wrapped the radiant gem in cloth and slipped out of the house. But the sins of the wicked can never stay hidden. Soldiers spotted him fleeing and gave chase. The thief, already weakened by his self-imposed starvation, could not outrun them. In desperation he ran back to Jinendrabhakt — who had just returned — and threw himself at the merchant's feet, crying, "Save me! Save me!"

Jinendrabhakt heard the soldiers shouting "A thief is escaping!" and understood at once that this man was no true ascetic but a fraud who preyed on people's trust. Yet in that critical moment, a greater fear gripped him: if this impostor were exposed in ascetic robes, the public would lose faith in the entire monastic order. The reputation of the dharma itself would suffer.

Protecting the Faith

So Jinendrabhakt turned to the soldiers and said calmly, "You are mistaken. This is no thief but a revered sage of spotless character. The gem he carries was given by my own instruction. You should be more careful before accusing a holy man."

The soldiers, chastened, bowed and withdrew. Once they were gone, Jinendrabhakt took the gem from the thief and spoke to him privately and firmly: "It is deeply shameful that you wear this sacred robe and defile it with such vile acts. Remember, by committing such sins you condemn yourself to endless suffering in lower births. The scriptures warn that those who abandon righteousness to fill their bellies will drown in the ocean of worldly existence for eternity. You have squandered this precious human life. Repent, and reform."

Having taught him thus, Jinendrabhakt sent him away. The thief slunk off, humbled by the mercy and wisdom of the man he had tried to rob.

The Teaching

This is the essence of upaguhana: when individuals within the faith stumble, the wise protect the honour of the dharma itself rather than exposing its followers to public scorn. The Jina's teaching is pure and blameless. Those who try to tarnish it are foolish — like a person with a bitter tongue who finds even sweet milk distasteful. The fault lies not in the milk, but in the tongue.
